reference.source: Respiratory and pulmonary vascular medicine references
clinicalPearls: Rare paraneoplastic pulmonary vasculopathy, most often complicating adenocarcinoma; gastric primaries are classic, with breast and lung also reported.
Tumour microemboli lodge in small pulmonary arteries and arterioles, triggering local coagulation and a fibrocellular intimal proliferation.
It is more than mechanical embolism; the reactive intimal proliferation and luminal narrowing drive the haemodynamic collapse.
Presents with subacute but rapidly progressive dyspnoea, dry cough and hypoxaemia.
Produces precapillary pulmonary hypertension and acute right heart failure.
Large pulmonary vessels are characteristically spared, so CT pulmonary angiography is often unremarkable, a key diagnostic trap.
Vascular endothelial growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor, tissue factor and osteopontin are implicated in the intimal remodelling.
Often diagnosed only at autopsy; ante-mortem diagnosis demands a high index of suspicion.
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy is a paraneoplastic pulmonary vasculopathy in which circulating tumour cells, most often from a gastric or other adenocarcinoma, lodge as microemboli within small pulmonary arteries and arterioles. Rather than causing purely mechanical obstruction, the tumour cells and adherent platelets activate the coagulation cascade through tissue factor and release growth factors including vascular endothelial growth factor and platelet-derived growth factor, stimulating a fibrocellular intimal proliferation with concentric luminal narrowing. Widespread microvascular occlusion rapidly raises pulmonary vascular resistance, producing precapillary pulmonary hypertension and acute right ventricular failure, and a consumptive coagulopathy with microangiopathic haemolysis may accompany the process. Because the large pulmonary vessels are characteristically spared, standard CT pulmonary angiography is often unremarkable despite a fulminant clinical course.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary tumour embolism without intimal proliferation
Idiopathic or other pulmonary arterial hypertension
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and other thrombotic microangiopathies
Interstitial lung disease or atypical infection
additionalInvestigations: CT pulmonary angiography (often negative for large emboli; may show ground-glass change, tree-in-bud or septal thickening)
Echocardiography demonstrating raised right heart pressures and right ventricular dilatation or strain
Blood film for schistocytes with haemolysis markers (lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin) and a coagulation/DIC screen
Right heart catheterisation confirming precapillary pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary microvascular cytology from a wedged pulmonary artery catheter
Search for an occult primary (upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, cross-sectional imaging, tumour markers)
Lung biopsy or post-mortem histology for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: Rapidly progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemia with a CT pulmonary angiogram negative for large emboli
Signs of acute right heart failure or exertional syncope
Unexplained pulmonary hypertension in a patient with known or suspected adenocarcinoma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is extremely poor, with survival often measured in days to weeks from symptom onset and the diagnosis frequently made only at autopsy. Rare patients recognised early and treated with therapy directed at the underlying malignancy, with supportive pulmonary vasodilator or targeted measures, have survived longer.
pitfalls: Being falsely reassured by a negative CT pulmonary angiogram and attributing symptoms to conventional pulmonary embolism.
Failing to consider occult malignancy in new, rapidly progressive pulmonary hypertension.
Delaying because definitive tissue is difficult to obtain during life.
Overlooking coexisting microangiopathic haemolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
